experiment: Solar eclipse 1919 May 29, Sobral (Brazil): 4-inch lens (Greenwich party, Crommelin & Davidson), 7 plates
quote: The result from declinations is about twice the weight of that from right ascensions, so that the mean result is 1″·98 with a probable error of about ±0″·12.
location: p. 331 (§39 summary); derived on p. 306 (§21-22: 'thus the deflection at the limb is 1″·98'; 'The probable error of the result judging from the accordance of the separate determinations is about 6 per cent.')
reference: Dyson F. W., Eddington A. S., Davidson C. 1920, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. Lond. A 220, 291-333
notes: ±0.12 is a probable error (= 0.6745 sigma), so sigma = 0.18 arcsec; Harvey 1979 (Table III) lists this result as 1.98 ± 0.18. The '±0.16' in the draft and in some secondary sources (e.g. Goldoni & Stefanini 2020, arXiv:2002.01179) does not appear in the paper. Ratio to 1.75 arcsec = 1.13. Will 2014 Fig. 5 draws it only as an off-scale arrow at 1919. Scan read from archive.org item philtrans06337895.

experiment: Solar eclipse 1919 May 29, Sobral: 13-inch astrographic (Greenwich), 16 eclipse plates, declinations only
quote: There remain the Sobral astrographic plates which gave the deflection 0″·93 discordant by an amount much beyond the limits of its accidental error.
reference: Dyson F. W., Eddington A. S., Davidson C. 1920, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. Lond. A 220, 291-333
notes: No uncertainty was published (Harvey 1979: 'an unspecified, large error'). The value comes from solving for the plate scale on the eclipse plates; taking the scale change from refraction and aberration only, the same paper gets 1″·52 at the limb (p. 312). Given little weight because the images were distorted. The '0.93 ± 0.05' quoted by Everitt (1980) is not in the paper. Re-reduced by Harvey 1979 (1.55 ± 0.34). Not plotted by Will.

experiment: Solar eclipse 1919 May 29, Principe (Eddington & Cottingham): Oxford astrographic, 2 usable plates, 5 stars
quote: our result may be written 1″·61±0″·30.
location: p. 328 (§37); repeated p. 331 ('The deflection obtained was 1″·61. The probable error is about ±0″·30')
reference: Dyson F. W., Eddington A. S., Davidson C. 1920, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. Lond. A 220, 291-333
notes: Probable error (sigma = 0.44 arcsec). Includes ±0″·14 from the plate scale, which was taken from check-field plates rather than solved from the eclipse plates. Ratio 0.92 ± 0.17 (p.e.). Will 2014 Fig. 5 plots 0.92 with a bar up to 1.09, i.e. the probable error is drawn as the error bar.

experiment: 1919 Sobral 4-inch plates re-measured (Zeiss Ascorecard, RGO) and re-reduced in 1978-79; 5 eclipse + 5 comparison plates
quote: 4-inch plates measured on the Zeiss 1·90 ± 0·11
reference: Harvey G. M. 1979, The Observatory 99, 195-198 [ADS 1979Obs....99..195H]
notes: Standard errors ('Each value was assigned a weight equal to the reciprocal of the square of its standard error', p. 197). In the same table Dyson et al.'s 4-inch value is written 1·98 ± 0·18 (their probable error converted to a standard error). Background to the re-analysis: Kennefick 2007 (arXiv:0709.0685).

experiment: 1919 Sobral astrographic plates re-measured (Zeiss Ascorecard, RGO) in both coordinates; 9 eclipse + 9 comparison plates
quote: Where the previous reduction yielded a value of 0″·93 with an unspecified, large error, the new determination is 1″·55±0″·34.
reference: Harvey G. M. 1979, The Observatory 99, 195-198 [ADS 1979Obs....99..195H]
notes: This is the re-reduction named in the draft (no number was given there). Dyson et al. had measured these plates in declination only.

experiment: 1919 Sobral, Harvey's weighted mean of the re-reduced 4-inch and astrographic results
quote: Combining the two fresh determinations, weighted according to their standard errors, gives 1″·87±0″·13, a result which is just within one standard error of the predicted value.
reference: Harvey G. M. 1979, The Observatory 99, 195-198 [ADS 1979Obs....99..195H]
notes: Harvey's reference to Dyson et al. is miscited as 'Mem. R.A.S., 62, 291, 1919'; the paper is Phil. Trans. A 220, 291 (1920).

experiment: Solar eclipse 1922 Sep 21, Wallal (W. Australia): Lick 15-ft cameras, 4 plate pairs, 62-85 stars, Tahiti comparison plates
quote: Mean from four plates 1″.72±″.11
reference: Campbell W. W., Trumpler R. 1923, Lick Obs. Bull. 11, 41-54 (No. 346); same table in PASP 35, 158 (1923)
notes: Probable errors: p. 52 says 'only one of the seven results differing from it by more than its probable error'; the PASP version gives the table 'together with their probable errors'. Einstein value quoted as 1″.745. A solution using displacements 'corrected' with the check-field residuals gave 2″.05 (p. 54); the authors left that open until the 5-ft plates were measured. Will 2014 Fig. 5 plots 0.98 with a ±0.06 bar (the p.e.).

experiment: Solar eclipse 1922 Sep 21, Wallal: Lick pair of 5-ft cameras, 6 plates
quote: the observations of this instrument lead to a value of 1″.82±″.15 for the light deflection at the Sun's limb.
location: Summary item 3, p. 160; Table 9 ('Mean of all plates +1″.82±″.15'), p. 151
reference: Campbell W. W., Trumpler R. 1928, Lick Obs. Bull. 13, 130-160 (No. 397)
notes: Draft called the 1928 paper a 're-analysis 1.75 ± 0.09'. It actually analyses the second instrument (5-ft cameras), which gives 1.82 ± 0.15; 1.75 ± 0.09 is the combination of both instruments (next row). Probable errors throughout. Will 2014 Fig. 5 plots 1.04 with a bar from 0.95 up to the top of the panel (±0.09 = the p.e.). Same final results also in PASP 40, 130 (1928).

experiment: Solar eclipse 1922 Sep 21, Wallal: weighted mean of the Lick 15-ft (weight 2) and 5-ft (weight 1) results
quote: With this law the combined observations of the two instruments furnish a value of 1″.75±″.09 for the deflection at the Sun's limb which agrees exactly with Einstein's prediction.
location: Summary item 7, p. 160; table on p. 151 ('Mean ... 1″.75±.09 (weight 3)')
reference: Campbell W. W., Trumpler R. 1928, Lick Obs. Bull. 13, 130-160 (No. 397)
notes: Not a re-analysis: the 2:1 weighted mean of 1.72 ± 0.11 (1923) and 1.82 ± 0.15 (1928). p. 151: 'the probable error of the final result of our observations is only 5 per cent.' Not plotted separately by Will. Do not plot together with the two rows above (same data).

experiment: Solar eclipse 1922 Sep 21, Wallal: Canadian party (Chant, Young), 11-ft camera, 2 plates, 18 stars
location: Summary table, p. 283 (columns: x co-ordinate, y co-ordinate, weighted mean)
reference: Chant C. A., Young R. K. 1923, Publ. Dominion Astrophys. Obs. Victoria 2, 275-285 (No. 15) [ADS 1923PDAO....2..275C]
notes: Draft had 'Chant & Young 1924 (Toronto)'; the report appeared in 1923 in Publ. DAO Victoria (ADS 1923PDAO....2..275C). No uncertainty given: three solutions give 1.75 (all stars), 1.42 and 2.16 arcsec depending on which discordant stars are dropped. The abstract only says the results are 'in harmony with' Einstein. Not plotted by Will; better shown as a range than as a point.

experiment: Solar eclipse 1922 Sep 21, Cordillo Downs (South Australia): Dodwell (Adelaide) & Davidson (Greenwich); 4 eclipse plates, result from plates I and II only
quote: General Mean 1″·77. ... The probable error of the final result may be taken as ±0″·3.
reference: Dodwell G. F., Davidson C. R. 1924, MNRAS 84, 150-162
notes: Draft named the paper without a value. Plate I gave 2.36, plate II 1.18 arcsec (mean of x and y). Probable error, so sigma is about 0.44 arcsec. Not plotted by Will.

experiment: Solar eclipse 1929 May 9, Takengon (N. Sumatra): Potsdam expedition, 8.5-m horizontal double camera, 4 plate pairs
quote: Mittel E = 2″,24 ± 0″,10, gemittelt nach Maßgabe der natürlichen Gewichte
reference: Freundlich E., v. Klüber H., v. Brunn A. 1931, Z. Astrophys. 3, 171-198 [ADS 1931ZA......3..171F]
notes: The ± is a German 'mittlerer Fehler' (mean error, i.e. 1 sigma); p. 188 speaks of 'einem mittleren Fehler von ± 0″,2 der Einzelbestimmung'. The four plates gave 2.25 ± 0.19, 2.17 ± 0.20, 2.61 ± 0.26 and 1.81 ± 0.19. The scale came from a collimator. The paper also argues that the 1919 and 1922 data, re-reduced, give about 2.2. Mikhailov (1959) re-reduced the plates with the scale solved from the stars and got 1.96 ± 0.08 (p.e.). Will Fig. 5: off-scale arrow at 1929.

experiment: Solar eclipse 1936 Jun 19, Kuibyshevka (USSR): Mikhailov, 6-m astrograph with a plane-parallel plate imaging a reference field, 2 plates, 29 stars
quote: 1936 | 2 | 29 | 2·0–7·2 | 29 | 0·27 | 2·70 | 2·68±0·37 (columns: year, plates, stars, limits of r, scale, p.e. of one star, A as given by observer, A new reduction)
reference: Original 1930s Soviet publication not accessed; value as listed by the observer himself in Mikhailov A. A. 1959, MNRAS 119, 593-608 (George Darwin Lecture)
notes: The draft's 2.73 ± 0.31 could not be found in any accessible source. In his own 1959 English-language account Mikhailov lists 2″·70 as 'given by observer' and gives a new reduction of 2″·68 ± 0″·37 (p.e.; next row). 2.73 ± 0.31 may come from the original publication, but I could not check it. Will Fig. 5: off-scale arrow at 1936.

experiment: 1936 Kuibyshevka plates, least-squares re-reduction by the observer (published 1959)
quote: A least squares solution of the equations of condition gave an unusually large value for A = 2″·68 ± 0″·37
reference: Mikhailov A. A. 1959, MNRAS 119, 593-608 (George Darwin Lecture)
notes: Mikhailov quotes probable errors throughout (e.g. 'A = 2″·07 ± 0″·09 p.e.' for his 1919 re-reduction; Table I weighted mean '1″·93 ± 0″·05 p.e.'). The reference-field (check-star) scale method failed (Mikhailov blames field rotation from the guiding), and the comparison plates were taken in March 1937 at -21 C, so the scale had to be solved from the eclipse stars.

experiment: Solar eclipse 1936 Jun 19, Kosimizu (Hokkaido): Tohoku Imperial University party (Matukuma), 1 eclipse plate, 8 measurable stars
quote: The average deflection value was 1, 71 arcsec. (Goldoni & Stefanini 2020, §2.2 - secondary)
reference: Matukuma T. 1941, Japanese J. Astron. Geophys. 18, 51-72 (not accessed); short report Nature 146, 264 (1940) (paywalled; free preview has no numbers)
notes: Draft mentioned 'Matukuma (Japan)' without a value. Primary not accessible; per the secondary source, one of the two comparison plates was unreliable. Not plotted by Will.

experiment: Solar eclipse 1947 May 20, Bocaiuva (Brazil): van Biesbroeck, Yerkes 20-ft camera, 1 eclipse plate, 51 stars
reference: van Biesbroeck G. 1950, AJ 55, 49-53
notes: m.e. = mean error (1 sigma). ADS's scan of 1950AJ.....55...49V stops at p. 52; p. 53 with the result is inside the scan of the next article (1950AJ.....55...53V). The auxiliary-field mirror was warped, so the scale had to be solved from the eclipse field, where no star was closer than 2.3 solar radii to the Sun's edge. Mikhailov (1959) gives it as ±0″·18 p.e. (= 0.27 × 0.6745) and re-reduces to 2.20 ± 0.38 p.e. Will Fig. 5: off-scale arrow plotted at about 1950.

experiment: Solar eclipse 1952 Feb 25, Khartoum (Sudan): van Biesbroeck, same Yerkes camera, 2 plates, 9-11 stars
quote: Giving half weight to the shorter first exposure which shows the poorer images and the smaller number of stars the average of 1″.70 ± ″.10 (m.e.) comes out close to the theoretical prediction 1″.75.
reference: van Biesbroeck G. 1953, AJ 58, 87-88
notes: m.e. = 1 sigma. Mikhailov (1959) re-reduced the published measures and got 1.43 ± 0.18 (p.e.); he also quotes the original as ±0″·07 p.e. (converted). Will Fig. 5: 0.97 ± 0.06.

experiment: Solar eclipse 1973 Jun 30, Chinguetti (Mauritania): Texas Mauritanian Eclipse Team (Texas-Princeton)
quote: The final value is L=(0.95±0.11) L_E, where the error is 1σ and L_E=1″.75 is Einstein's value.
reference: Texas Mauritanian Eclipse Team 1976, AJ 81, 452-454
notes: Companion paper Jones 1976 (next row) gives the arcsec value and the reduction details. Will Fig. 5: 0.95 (+0.11; lower bar clipped by the panel).

experiment: Solar eclipse 1973 Jun 30, Chinguetti: plate reductions (RGO Galaxy machine), 39 stars within 9 solar radii
quote: Thus, our final result is L=1.66±0.18 arcsec. The error does not take into account a possible wrong choice of the light deflection in determining the scale change.
notes: Same measurement as the row above (do not plot both). Abstract: 'L = (0.95 ± 0.11 std. dev.) L_E'. 1.66/1.75 = 0.949 and 0.18/1.75 = 0.103, so the papers round the ratio error up to 0.11. The error combines the least-squares error with the scale error (Table II).

experiment: Solar eclipse 2017 Aug 21, Wyoming: amateur-class refractor + CCD (Bruns), 45 images, star positions from UCAC5
quote: The final result was a deflection coefficient L = 1.752 arcsec, compared to the theoretical value of L = 1.751 arcsec, with an uncertainty of only 3%.
location: abstract; §1: 'The calculated uncertainty is only 3.4%, suggesting the deflection coefficient L is likely to be between 1.69 arcsec and 1.81 arcsec.'
reference: Bruns D. G. 2018, Class. Quantum Grav. 35, 075009
notes: Not in the draft. Only the arXiv v1 was read. The ±0.06 is the stated 3.4% (range 1.69-1.81 arcsec); the confidence level is not stated. The errors are 3.1% from the star fit and 1.23% from the independent plate-scale calibration. Ratio 1.001 ± 0.034. The only modern optical eclipse result I found; it is not in Will 2014.

experiment: Occultation of 3C 279 by the Sun, Oct 1969: Owens Valley (Caltech) interferometer, 9.602 GHz
quote: Rapid instrumental calibration and negligible coronal diffraction enabled the measurement of a general relativity deflection of 1.77″±0.20″ at the limb of the sun.
reference: Seielstad G. A., Sramek R. A., Weiler K. W. 1970, Phys. Rev. Lett. 24, 1373
notes: Draft named the paper without a value. Full text paywalled; the abstract (APS page) does not state the error convention. Sramek 1971 describes both 1969 results as having 'standard deviations of about 10 percent'. Hill 1971 and Fomalont & Sramek 1977 list it as a ratio, 1.01 ± 0.11. Will Fig. 5: 1.01 at 1969.

experiment: Occultation of 3C 279, Oct 1969: JPL Goldstone interferometer, 2.4 GHz, 21.57-km baseline
quote: The observed deflection was 1.04 (+0.15, -0.10) times that predicted by Einstein's theory of general relativity.
reference: Muhleman D. O., Ekers R. D., Fomalont E. B. 1970, Phys. Rev. Lett. 24, 1377
notes: Draft named the paper without a value. Asymmetric error, convention not stated in the abstract. Will Fig. 5: 1.04 at 1969.

experiment: Occultation of 3C 279, Oct 1970: Goldstone-Haystack VLBI, 7.8 GHz, 3900-km baseline (Shapiro et al.)
location: secondary: Fomalont & Sramek 1977, Table I, p. 24
reference: I. I. Shapiro, result 'as listed in Gravitation and Cosmology by Steven Weinberg (Wiley 1972), p. 194' (per Fomalont E. B., Sramek R. A. 1977, Comments Astrophys. 7, 19-33 [ADS 1977ComAp...7...19F]); not accessed
notes: Not in the draft. This is the 1.03 point plotted at 1970 in Will 2014 Fig. 5.

experiment: Occultation of 3C 279, Oct 1970: NRAO Green Bank 3-element interferometer (2.7 km), 2.695 + 8.085 GHz (first dual-frequency coronal correction)
quote: After correcting for this refraction, the gravitational bending was found to be 1″.57 ± 0″.08 at the limb of the Sun. This is 0.90 ± 0.05 of the deflection predicted by Einstein's general theory of relativity.
location: abstract, p. L55; Table 1 (noise error ±0.06, total ±0.08 arcsec)
reference: Sramek R. A. 1971, ApJ 167, L55-L60
notes: Draft named 'Sramek 1971/1974' without values. Errors are 'formal standard deviations' from the phase noise, plus a coronal-model term. Fomalont & Sramek (1975) cite a 'revised error determination, Sramek 1974' (Varenna 'Enrico Fermi' school, July 1972), which I could not access; Fomalont & Sramek 1977 still list 0.90 ± 0.05. Will Fig. 5: 0.90 at 1970.

experiment: Occultation of 3C 279, Oct 1970: Cambridge One-Mile telescope, 2.7 + 5.0 GHz, 1.41-km baseline
quote: The observed deflection was 1·07 ± 0·17 times that predicted by General Relativity.
location: Summary, p. 7P; p. 9P: 'deflections due to the Sun of 1·07 ±0·17 (s.e.) and 1·14 ±0·30 (s.e.) respectively' (large and small baselines)
reference: Hill J. M. 1971, MNRAS 153, 7P-11P
notes: Draft named 'Hill 1971' without a value. The 0.66-km baseline gave 1.14 ± 0.30 (s.e.). Will Fig. 5: 1.07 at 1970.

experiment: Occultation of 3C 279, Oct 1971: NRAO 2.7-km interferometer, 8.1 + 2.7 GHz
location: secondary: Fomalont & Sramek 1977, Table I, p. 24
reference: Sramek R. A. 1974, Proc. Int. School of Physics 'Enrico Fermi', Course 56, Varenna, July 1972 (not accessed); listed in Fomalont E. B., Sramek R. A. 1977, Comments Astrophys. 7, 19-33 [ADS 1977ComAp...7...19F]
notes: This is the 0.97 point plotted at 1971 in Will 2014 Fig. 5.

experiment: Occultation of 3C 279, Oct 1972: Cambridge 5-km telescope, 5.0 GHz (3C 279 vs 3C 48)
quote: The observed deflection was 1·04 ± 0·08 times that predicted by General Relativity.
location: Summary, p. 11P; text p. 13P: 'λ = 1·02 ± 0·08 (standard deviation) without the coronal refraction correction and 1·04 ± 0·08 with it.'
reference: Riley J. M. 1973, MNRAS 161, 11P-14P
notes: Not in the draft. Will Fig. 5: 1.04 at 1972.

experiment: Occultation of 3C 279, Oct 1972: Westerbork Synthesis Radio Telescope, 4995 MHz (single frequency, coronal model)
quote: The measured gravitational deflection was then 0.96±0.05 times the value predicted by General Relativity.
location: Summary, p. 241; p. 248: 'consistent with ... General Relativity within one standard deviation'
reference: Weiler K. W., Ekers R. D., Raimond E., Wellington K. J. 1974, A&A 30, 241-248 [ADS 1974A&A....30..241W]
notes: Draft named 'Weiler et al. 1974/1975' without values. Will Fig. 5: 0.96 at 1972.

experiment: Occultation of 3C 279, Oct 1972: four-antenna VLBI on an 845-km baseline (NRAO-Haystack), 3.7 cm, 3C 279 and 3C 273B observed simultaneously
quote: ...yielded a gravitational deflection of 0.99±0.03 times the value predicted by general relativity, corresponding to γ=0.98±0.06 (standard error).
reference: Counselman C. C. III, Kent S. M., Knight C. A., Shapiro I. I., Clark T. A., Hinteregger H. F., Rogers A. E. E., Whitney A. R. 1974, Phys. Rev. Lett. 33, 1621
notes: Draft named the paper without a value. VLBI, but Will groups it with the 'Radio' points (0.99 at 1972).

experiment: Occultation of 3C 279, Oct 1973: Westerbork, 5.0 + 1.4 GHz
quote: The gravitational bending measured was 1.038±0.033 times that predicted by general relativity.
reference: Weiler K. W., Ekers R. D., Raimond E., Wellington K. J. 1975, Phys. Rev. Lett. 35, 134
notes: Error convention not stated in the abstract (full text paywalled). Will Fig. 5: 1.04 at 1973.

quote: The measured bending in terms of that at the solar limb is 1″.775 ± 0″.019 (standard error), or 1.015 ± 0.011 times the Einstein prediction of general relativity.
reference: Fomalont E. B., Sramek R. A. 1975, ApJ 199, 749-755
notes: The draft's '1.015 ± 0.011' belongs to this 1975 ApJ paper (1974 data), not to the 1976 PRL. Will Fig. 5: 1.01 at 1974.

experiment: NRAO 35-km interferometer, same three sources (Mar-Apr 1975 experiment alone)
quote: 1.015 ± 0.011 in 1974 / 0.999 ± 0.011 in 1975 / 1.007 ± 0.009 average. The errors are one standard deviation and the combined result assumed that the two determinations are independent.
location: Fomalont & Sramek 1977, p. 27; also Table I, p. 24 (citing the 1976 PRL)
reference: Fomalont E. B., Sramek R. A. 1977, Comments Astrophys. 7, 19-33 [ADS 1977ComAp...7...19F]
notes: This 1975-only value is the 1.00 ± 0.012 point plotted at 1975 in Will 2014 Fig. 5. Do not plot together with the 1974+1975 mean (next row).

experiment: NRAO 35-km interferometer: mean of the 1974 and 1975 experiments
quote: The mean gravitational deflection is 1.007 ± 0.009 (standard error) times the value predicted by general relativity.
reference: Fomalont E. B., Sramek R. A. 1976, Phys. Rev. Lett. 36, 1475
notes: The draft listed '(1+γ)/2 = 1.015 ± 0.011?' against both the 1975 ApJ and this 1976 PRL; this paper gives 1.007 ± 0.009 (1974 and 1975 combined). The 1977 review restates the same result as 1.761 ± 0.016 arcsec at the limb and γ = 1.014 ± 0.018 (p. 31-32).

experiment: Geodetic VLBI data (less than 4 years of observations)
quote: We now report the most sensitive measurement of deflection so far achieved, in which very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) observations yield a value of γ of 1.008 with a 1 σ formal standard error of ±0.005.
reference: Robertson D. S., Carter W. E. 1984, Nature 310, 572
notes: Draft named the paper without a value. Formal 1 sigma. (1+γ)/2 = 1.004 ± 0.0025. Will Fig. 5 draws this at 1.000 ± about 0.005 (1984). Data span from Lambert & Le Poncin-Lafitte 2009.

experiment: Geodetic VLBI, ten years of data, sources 2.5°-178° from the Sun
quote: Our analysis of ten years of VLBI data, including observations of objects in the range 2.5° < α < 178°, yields an estimate γ = 1.0002 with a formal standard error of 0.00096 and an estimated standard error of 0.002.
reference: Robertson D. S., Carter W. E., Dillinger W. H. 1991, Nature 349, 768
notes: Draft named the paper without a value. 0.002 is the 'estimated standard error'; the formal error is 0.00096. Will Fig. 5: arrows at 1990.

experiment: VLBI on 3C 273B and 3C 279 around the Oct 1987 occultation of 3C 279 (antennas in California and Massachusetts), 2, 8 and 23 GHz
quote: ...from which we obtained γ = 0.9996 ± 0.0017 (estimated standard error), corresponding to a gravitational deflection 0.9998 ± 0.0008 times that predicted by general relativity.
reference: Lebach D. E., Corey B. E., Shapiro I. I., Ratner M. I., Webber J. C., Rogers A. E. E., Davis J. L., Herring T. A. 1995, Phys. Rev. Lett. 75, 1439
notes: Draft (copied from Will 2014 §3.4.1) gives γ−1 = (−8 ± 34)×10^-4. The paper gives γ−1 = (−4 ± 17)×10^-4, i.e. (1+γ)/2 = 0.9998 ± 0.0008. Will's numbers are exactly twice the published ones, which is what you get by mistaking 0.9996 ± 0.0017 for (1+γ)/2. Fomalont et al. 2009 and Froeschlé et al. 1997 quote the paper correctly. 'Estimated standard error' = realistic 1 sigma.

experiment: Geodetic VLBI data base 1979-1999
quote: Using a large geodetic VLBI data set, we obtained γ = 0.9998₃ ± 0.0004₅ (estimated standard error).
reference: Shapiro S. S., Davis J. L., Lebach D. E., Gregory J. S. 2004, Phys. Rev. Lett. 92, 121101
notes: The abstract prints the last digit of value and error as subscripts (0.9998_3 ± 0.0004_5 = 0.99983 ± 0.00045). Lambert & Le Poncin-Lafitte 2009 quote the statistical (formal) standard error, 0.00026. Will 2014: (1+γ)/2 = 0.99992 ± 0.00023, γ−1 = (−1.7 ± 4.5)×10^-4. Will Fig. 5: '2×10^-4' arrows at 2004.

experiment: VLBA phase-referenced observations of 3C 279 and three nearby sources, 18 days in Oct 2005, 43/23/15 GHz
quote: ...we have determined the deflection parameter γ = 0.9998 ± 0.0003 (68% confidence level), in agreement with General Relativity.
location: abstract; §5 (average of the four solutions in Table 5)
reference: Fomalont E., Kopeikin S., Lanyi G., Benson J. 2009, ApJ 699, 1395-1402

experiment: Geodetic VLBI 1979-2008: 3,937 sessions, 4.39 million delays, 988 sources (global solution)
reference: Lambert S. B., Le Poncin-Lafitte C. 2009, A&A 499, 331-335
notes: The draft listed this paper but gave only the 2011 number. The abstract gives no single value; it concludes 'γ cannot be estimated at better than 2 × 10^-4'. Other time spans in Table 1 range from 0.99940 to 1.00031. Will 2014's γ−1 = (−1.6 ± 1.5)×10^-4 is this row. Probably the '10^-4' arrow pair at about 2008 in Will's Fig. 5, although Fomalont et al. 2009 would carry the same label.

experiment: Geodetic VLBI Aug 1979-Aug 2010: more than 7 million group delays (incl. VLBA RDV and VCS sessions), global solution
quote: The most complete solution of this study yielded γ = 0.99992 ± 0.00012, whereas it was 0.99984 ± 0.00015 in our 2009 paper.
reference: Lambert S. B., Le Poncin-Lafitte C. 2011, A&A 529, A70
notes: Formal error (abstract: 'the formal error in γ decreases when additional sessions are processed'). Not on arXiv; read from HAL hal-03785812.

experiment: Dedicated geodetic VLBI session AUA020 (1 May 2017): 0229+131 and 0235+164 at 1-3° from the Sun
quote: OCCAM | All stations | Both | 0.53 | 1.14 | 0.34 | 28 (Table 1, units 10^-4)
reference: Titov O. et al. 2018, A&A 618, A8
notes: Draft asked 'γ?'. The paper gives no single headline value. Other single-session solutions in Table 1: Sejong down-weighted (OCCAM) 0.89 ± 0.94; Calc/Solve −0.26 ± 1.09 (×10^-4). Formal errors 0.9-4 ×10^-4.

experiment: Global solution over 6,301 geodetic VLBI sessions (12.6 million ionosphere-free delays), parameterised as in Lambert & Le Poncin-Lafitte
quote: We obtained γ − 1 = (2.72 ± 0.92) × 10−4 that yields a slight improvement with respect to Lambert & Le Poncin-Lafitte (2011)
reference: Titov O. et al. 2018, A&A 618, A8
notes: Three sigma from GR; the authors say 'these global solutions exhibit systematics at the level of 2-3σ'. Removing session AUA020 gives (2.57 ± 0.97)×10^-4. Not recommended for plotting. No newer VLBI γ value was found (the 2019 proceedings, arXiv:1908.00973, repeat these results).

experiment: Hipparcos: all FAST and NDAC star-abscissa residuals from the 37-month mission; stars 47°-133° from the Sun
quote: From the results we can conclude that the coefficient γ is within 0.3 per cent of unity, with γ = 0.997 ± 0.003.
reference: Froeschlé M., Mignard F., Arenou F. 1997, in Hipparcos - Venice '97, ESA SP-402, p. 49-52 [ADS 1997ESASP.402...49F]
notes: The Greek gamma is lost from the PDF text layer; the meaning is unambiguous. Formal error (§4.2: 'As long as one can consider the formal error as representative of a true uncertainty'); the -0.92 correlation with the global parallax zero point inflates it by about 2.5. ADS scan filed under 1997hipp.conf...49F. Will Fig. 5: 'Hipparcos' arrows at about 1998. No Gaia measurement of γ has been published (see notes file).

experiment: Planetary radar echo delays near superior conjunction (MIT; Mercury, 1966-67)
quote: (secondary) 'From 12 measurements around the mid-May superior conjunction, and 7 measurements around the following superior conjunction in late August, the astronomers obtained a measurement of γ = 0.8 ± 0.4' (Pössel 2021)
location: secondary: Pössel 2021, arXiv:2110.07016, eq. (24); Will 2014 Fig. 5 bar at 1968 (top at 1.10, lower end clipped)

quote: The corresponding value for the metric parameter γ is 1.000 ± 0.002, where the quoted uncertainty, twice the formal standard deviation, allows for possible systematic errors.
reference: Reasenberg R. D., Shapiro I. I., MacNeil P. E., Goldstein R. B., Breidenthal J. C., Brenkle J. P., Cain D. L., Kaufman T. M., Komarek T. A., Zygielbaum A. I. 1979, ApJ 234, L219-L221

experiment: Cassini two-way X/Ka-band Doppler around the June 2002 solar conjunction (spacecraft 8.43 AU from the Earth and 7.42 AU from the Sun, closest ray 1.6 solar radii; Will 2014 says 8.43 AU from the Sun)
quote: Our result, γ = 1 + (2.1 ± 2.3) × 10−5, agrees with the predictions of standard general relativity
reference: Bertotti B., Iess L., Tortora P. 2003, Nature 425, 374-376
notes: Value verified from the abstract. The abstract does not state the error convention and the Nature full text was not accessible. It is 1 sigma (formal) according to the same group: Bertotti, Ashby & Iess 2008, CQG 25, 045013 (arXiv:0709.1512) write 'the formal accuracy 2.3 × 10^-5 in γ'; Kopeikin et al. 2007 (arXiv:gr-qc/0604060) call it 'the quoted standard deviation σγ = 2.3 × 10^-5'. The measurement is of the Doppler (frequency) shift, i.e. the time derivative of the delay. (1+γ)/2 − 1 = (1.05 ± 1.15)×10^-5. Geometry: 8.43 AU is the Earth-Cassini distance (Nature Fig. 1), not the heliocentric one as Will 2014 has it; JPL Horizons gives 7.42 AU from the Sun. Closest ray 1.6 solar radii (Ashby & Bertotti 2010, CQG 27, 145013, p. 3), which also states the error explicitly as 'at 1-σ' (eq. 1).

experiment: INPOP10a planetary ephemeris (incl. MESSENGER Mercury flybys); γ varied with β fixed to 1
reference: Fienga A., Laskar J., Kuchynka P., Manche H., Desvignes G., Gastineau M., Cognard I., Theureau G. 2011, Celest. Mech. Dyn. Astron. 111, 363-385
notes: β fixed to 1. The interval is the range of γ for which the post-fit residuals change by less than 5% relative to INPOP10a; it is not a sigma. Fienga et al. 2015 (arXiv:1409.4932, Table 2) and Fienga & Minazzoli 2024 (LRR 27, 1, Table 5) list INPOP10a as γ−1 = (−6.2 ± 8.1)×10^-5. That number is the β−1 of the γ = 1 run in the same Table 4 (−0.62 ± 0.81 ×10^-4), so it looks like a transcription error. Verma et al. 2014 and Pitjeva & Pitjev 2013 quote (4.5 ± 7.5)×10^-5, which matches this row.

experiment: EPM2011 ephemeris: about 678,000 observations 1913-2011 (mostly radar/laser ranging); β, γ, J2 and other parameters fitted together
reference: Pitjeva E. V., Pitjev N. P. 2013, MNRAS 432, 3431-3437
notes: Simultaneous fit, with J2 = (2.0 ± 0.2)×10^-7 (3σ). The paper contradicts itself on the error level: eq. (3) says '(3σ)' but the Conclusion repeats the same numbers with '(σ)'. I recorded 3σ from the Results section; the sibling beta_lunar.csv records the same pair as 'realistic'. 'Pitjeva & Pitjev 2014' (CeMDA 119, 237) was not accessed, and the 2024 Living Review lists no γ value from it.

experiment: INPOP13a with 1.5 yr of MESSENGER orbital radio-science range; β and γ varied together
reference: Verma A. K., Fienga A., Laskar J., Manche H., Gastineau M. 2014, A&A 561, A115
notes: Interval where the post-fit residuals change by less than 25%. Tighter thresholds give 10%: (0.0 ± 1.1)×10^-5 and 5%: (0.0 ± 0.18)×10^-5. The direct least-squares fit (1σ formal, 'very optimistic') gives γ−1 = (4.53 ± 0.54)×10^-5. Fienga & Minazzoli 2024 label this result 'INPOP13c' and 'FF' (full fit).
